The Mackenzie River. Canada's largest river by discharge, it flows approximately one thousand twenty-five miles northwestward from Great Slave Lake to the Arctic Ocean. One of North America's great Arctic waterways, the Mackenzie originates where Great Slave Lake spills out into the Northwest Territories and drains a vast expanse of Canada's northern interior. The river was named after Alexander Mackenzie, the Scottish-Canadian fur trader who explored it in seventeen eighty-nine while searching for a route to the Pacific. From its source, the river flows northward through a landscape of tundra, muskeg, and boreal forest, eventually widening into a massive delta before emptying into the Arctic Ocean near Inuvik. It discharges more water into the Arctic Ocean than any other North American river, with enormous seasonal flooding during the brief Arctic summer. In winter the river freezes over completely, making it impassable for most of the year, though the spring breakup can be spectacular and destructive. Historically the lifeblood of the fur trade in northwestern Canada, the river supported Hudson's Bay Company posts all along its course. Today it remains home to diverse Arctic and subarctic fauna including muskrats and beavers, along with migratory fish species, and it continues to be critical habitat for the Dene and Métis peoples.
